item.title: Digital Overload and the Wellness Room Boom
item.description:
Environment

Digital Overload and the Wellness Room Boom

Are we digitally overfed and naturally undernourished?

Posted October 11, 2026

Key points
  • The rise of wellness rooms could reflect a growing desire for natural, calming, and restorative environments.
  • Research links exposure to real nature with improved well-being and stress reduction.
  • Virtual nature may offer benefits but research has yet to establish whether it can replicate the real thing.

Last holiday season, my husband and I gave family and friends alarm clocks designed to make waking and falling asleep more peaceful. The clocks simulate sunrise, play nature sounds, and tell bedtime stories. We thought they were great wellness gifts, but now I’m thinking twice. The clock requires an app and a subscription to recreate experiences humans have relied on for thousands of years: morning light, darkness at night, stars, birdsong, rain, and a soothing voice.

The trend toward curated wellness is showing up in both the products we buy and the spaces we create. According to Houzz’s 2026 Emerging Summer Trends Report, searches for “wellness rooms” rose 164%, while interest in “calming” spaces increased 139%. Searches for “biophilic design,” which incorporates natural elements into architecture and interior decor, rose 112% (Houzz, 2026). Wellness room images reveal a pattern: natural light, plants, warm wood, soft fabrics, and popular paint colors like “forest green, rain dance, white dove, and mushroom.”

Endless Stimulation, Not Necessarily Restoration

In a culture of constant stimulation, are we digitally overfed and naturally undernourished?

Modern life gives our senses plenty to process. Notifications compete for our attention, and screens glow long after sunset. Televisions, traffic, music, social media, and appliances create a nearly constant soundtrack. Scents are manufactured, and highly processed foods amplify sweetness, saltiness, and flavor. Our eyes move from phone to computer to television.

The natural world stimulates our senses differently. A breeze moves through trees, then stops. Leaves flutter, birds call, and light and temperature shift throughout the day. We feel variable wind, rain, humidity, coolness, and warmth from the sun. We might touch uneven ground, bark, sand, water, and other natural textures while smelling soil, rain, mown grass, flowers, or salt air. When outdoors, we experience countless subtle physical and sensory signals. Nature is complex, changing, and multisensory; something technology cannot exactly replicate… yet.

The health implications of artificial environments are emerging. A 2026 meta-analysis spanning 36 studies with 30 bird species found that artificial light at night was associated with reduced sleep, increased metabolic rate, accelerated reproductive maturation, and changes in daily activity (Diaz-Palma et al., 2026). Interestingly, these disruptions did not translate into measurable effects on survival, growth, or reproductive success (Diaz-Palma et al., 2026). The findings suggest that birds may adjust, even as their physiology and innate behaviors change.

Similar concerns about artificial lighting are evident in human research. A study involving 86,772 adults found that greater nighttime light exposure was associated with a higher likelihood of depression, anxiety, PTSD, and bipolar disorder (Burns et al., 2023). In an earlier study with over 400,000 adults, more time spent outdoors in daylight (self-reported) was associated with better mood, increased happiness, and fewer sleep difficulties (Burns et al., 2021). Although these two human studies were observational, they add to evidence that how we experience light matters.

Can We Replicate Nature?

When I worked in hospitals, I remember envying the smokers because they had permission to go outside every few hours. They could step away from the fluorescent lights, machines, sterile hallways, and constant demands. Even for a few minutes, they felt the outdoor air, natural light, and whatever greenery happened to be nearby.

A nurse friend recently told me about her hospital creating a room where healthcare workers could escape the stress of their shifts. Intrigued, I looked into the research and discovered a 2025 study involving 18 hospitals that converted underused spaces into “Recharge Rooms.” These rooms featured projected natural landscapes, imitation plants, essential oil diffusers, low lighting, music, and nature sounds (Cooke et al., 2025). After using the rooms, healthcare workers reported feeling less stressed, more hopeful and alert (Cooke et al., 2025). The study was not a randomized controlled trial so the results cannot establish causation, but the findings are intriguing.

The recharge rooms raise an interesting question: How does experiencing nature indoors compare with actually being outside?

In an earlier experiment, researchers compared six minutes in an actual forest with six minutes watching a video of the same forest through a 360-degree virtual reality headset (Browning et al., 2020). Participants rated both experiences as more restorative than sitting indoors without nature. Importantly, positive mood increased after the outdoor experience, while remaining unchanged following the virtual experience (Browning et al., 2020).

In a more recent meta-analysis of 16 studies, researchers found that nature exposure improved perceived mental restoration and mood (Malibary et al., 2026). When they examined different forms of exposure separately, real nature showed a statistically significant benefit, while artificial and virtual nature did not (Malibary et al., 2026). However, because there were so few studies on simulated nature, it cannot be concluded that being outside is definitely better.

More research is needed to better understand how closely simulated nature can replicate the restorative benefits of the real thing. Or, maybe, instead of trying to recreate nature indoors, we could all make an effort to spend more time outdoors whenever possible.

What Are You Feeding Your Senses?

I know most of us do not have extra space for a wellness room or regular access to a forest, or even a park. But, we can begin by noticing our everyday sensory environments and find small ways to bring in organic aspects of the natural world.

Where does natural light enter your indoor space? Can you position yourself so you see the sky or trees? Can you open a window and feel the breeze or listen for natural sounds? Do you have ways to experience quiet, darkness, changing temperatures, and natural textures? Can you introduce more live plants to your space? Can you step outside more often throughout your day?

For years, we have paid attention to what we feed our bodies and minds. The “wellness room boom” may be inviting us to consider what we are feeding our senses and whether we can find natural sources, rather than artificial, tech-based substitutes, to fully nourish ourselves.

item.title: Why "I'm Sorry You Feel This Way" Adds Insult to Injury
item.description:
Guilt

Why "I'm Sorry You Feel This Way" Adds Insult to Injury

Our decency should be stronger than our fear of admitting a mistake.

Posted October 11, 2026

Key points
  • “I’m sorry you feel this way” shifts the problem from what the speaker did to how the listener feels.
  • If you did nothing wrong, honest disagreement is more respectful than a counterfeit apology.
  • If you caused the harm, name what you did rather than apologizing for the other person’s feelings.

"I am sorry you feel this way." We have all heard the sentence, and felt the sting of it.

We are all psychologically aware enough to know that feelings can reflect very little of what actually happens. Our feelings are our feelings, and we can feel them independent of the world around us. The fact that someone else feels angry doesn't mean I did wrong; feelings are not proof of anything or objective evidence.

When a 6-foot-5, 240-pound heavyweight professional boxer suffers from spider phobia in a country where there are no venomous spiders and the largest ones are smaller than a quarter, his fear doesn't make spiders dangerous. "I am sorry you feel this way" plays on the same psychological script: It is your problem that you feel how you feel. However, this statement masquerades as an apology.

Read the grammar slowly: In a real apology, the speaker is the subject and the act is the object: I did this. In "I'm sorry you feel this way," the speaker's act has disappeared. What remains is the listener's feeling, now standing where the wrongdoing used to be.

Call it the change-of-address apology as the harm has been moved. It no longer lives in what was said or done. It lives in you, your reaction, and the way you took it. The speaker expresses regret about the new location but keeps the old one locked.

The sentence lands as an insult rather than a repair because it borrows the vocabulary of apology while removing the element that injured parties expect and value most. There is a second cost: When a person's emotional response is treated as the thing that went wrong, the underlying message is that your reaction does not make sense.

If "I am sorry you feel this way" does all this damage, why is it so common? Often it's because it's a compromise. A full apology costs something; it requires admitting an act, and admitting an act can feel like admitting a flaw. "I'm sorry you feel this way" sits between those two doors. It lets the speaker feel kind without feeling guilty. In my clinical experience, many people learned it early, in homes where admitting fault meant punishment or humiliation, and where the safest move was to soothe a parent's mood without conceding anything. That strategy may have once worked to keep a child out of trouble but it does not hold up in adult relationships that run on accountability.

Context matters, too. If you did nothing wrong and someone is in pain, saying you are sorry they are hurting is sympathy, not evasion. The sentence becomes a non-apology when it follows a harm the speaker caused and is offered in place of owning it.

If you are on the receiving end of "I am sorry you feel this way." here is the reframe: the hollow feeling you experience is not oversensitivity but accurate perception. You noticed that something was missing because something was. That means you do not have to argue for the legitimacy of your feelings, a debate the change-of-address apology quietly invites and that you are unlikely to win. You can step around it: I'm not asking you to be sorry about my feelings. I'm asking whether you see what happened. The question returns the harm to its original address without raising the temperature.

article continues after advertisement

If you are the one sending the sentence, you are allowed not to apologize. If you genuinely believe you did nothing wrong, say so plainly and kindly: I can see this hurt you, and I see it differently. Honest disagreement respects the other person more than a counterfeit apology does. What corrodes trust is performative remorse with responsibility removed. And if you notice that you reach for this sentence often, that is worth getting curious about rather than ashamed of. Somewhere, it probably kept you safe. When dismissal becomes a pattern in close relationships, it can help to talk it through with a therapist or someone you trust outside that relationship.

All of this comes back to a single idea: An apology is, at bottom, a statement about location. It tells the other person where you believe the harm lives. A real apology places it in what you did. A counterfeit one puts in where they took it.

Should we ever reach for "I am sorry you feel this way"? Yes and no. We can employ it when we sincerely believe we did not do anything wrong. In such a case, "this is a misunderstanding" may also be a good option. But when we know we have caused the harm, the decent thing to do is to say what you did and let the apology go to its proper address.

item.title: Female Mass Shooters Are a Reality We Can't Afford to Ignore
item.description:
Mass Shootings

Female Mass Shooters Are a Reality We Can't Afford to Ignore

Sexism, media, and semantics take eyes off violent females, leading to tragedy.

Posted October 11, 2026

Key points
  • Males are not the only perpetrators of rampage, mass, and targeted shootings.
  • Sexism, media, and semantics lead to the underestimation of females' capacity for violence.
  • When a couple plots a mass or targeted attack, virtually 100% of the time the female is the primary planner.

When teaching others on threat assessment, I rely on post-incident analyses from past mass and targeted shootings, and show trainees and students photos of shooters from Columbine, Virginia Tech, Sandy Hook, and Marjorie Stoneman Douglas to prove a point. I don't caption the photos, yet every single time, those in attendance are able to identify the shooters by name. Sadly, they live in infamy, with some even having fan clubs on Discord and other social media sites. As an example, there is a group of youth, Columbiners, who admire the Columbine shooters to the extent they have their images tattooed on their bodies. They idolize the killers.

In a recent training, I showed attendees photos of several females who committed, or planned to commit, similar acts as the males identified above. Not a single attendee could identify any of the photos. In fact, some thought the females were victims rather than violent women.

The danger in this is that warning signs of dangerous females are missed or ignored, resulting in a greater likelihood of females slipping through the cracks and killing others in manners similar to the worst male perpetrators.

Semantics, Media, and Sexism

Three contributors to the misconception that females simply don't commit acts of mass or targeted violence are semantics, media, and sexism. Let's break that down. Related to semantics, people often utilize "mass," "rampage," and "targeted" killings interchangeably, which often leads to the exclusion of female shooter data from official counts because there tend to be fewer victims than the four or more needed to constitute a mass killing. This feeds right into media because coverage tends to focus on high-fatality, male-perpetrated incidents. Finally, sexism lends itself to the assumption that females who kill often do so under male influence or, when they do commit such acts, they are thought to be crimes of passion. All of this misinformation has led to warning signs being overlooked, resulting in tragedy.

What the Mind Can't Grasp

The possibility of a dangerous situation involving a female is often dismissed because we have been raised to believe that females don't commit school shootings. Kristy Gneiting, a teacher at Rigby Middle School, came face-to-face with a female student holding a gun, in the middle of a school day. The student had already shot three people, yet Ms. Gneiting's statement after the shooting was, "It was a little girl and my brain couldn't quite grasp that...I just knew when I saw that gun, I had to get the gun."

Gneiting's initial reaction reflected an ingrained misperception about the violent capabilities of females. She is a hero who eventually took action, but her initial confusion in the moment is an example of just how commonly real threats by females are missed and intervention opportunities are lost. Thankfully, she acted.

article continues after advertisement

The Numbers Might Surprise You

Although less than 3% of mass shootings are committed by females, other data might surprise you: 25% of rampage and targeted attacks involve females and, when a male and female plan an attack together, historically the female is the primary planner virtually 100% of the time with males following their lead.

The No Notoriety movement, created by the parents of Alex Teves, who died in the Aurora, Colorado movie theater shooting, is exactly the type of movement that takes the attention away from mass and targeted shooters. They do not deserve our attention. However, there are times when education lends itself to the necessity of naming perpetrators, such as when we want to be sure to prevent future tragedies.

The Truth About Female Perpetrators of Mass and Targeted Violence

There isn't enough space here to list all female mass and targeted killers, but I'd like to shed light on a few facts to make sure you have a full grasp of their capabilities, and potentially prevent future tragedies.

One of the first school shooters in the U.S. was Brenda Spencer, a 16-year-old girl who, in 1979, aimed a rifle toward Grover Cleveland Elementary School in San Diego, killed the principal and custodian, and injured eight children and a law enforcement officer. When asked why, she coldly replied, "I don't like Mondays." Other female-perpetrated rampage, mass, and targeted killings have taken place in schools, malls, the post office, Kraft Foods, the University of Alabama, YouTube headquarters, among other locations. In addition, numerous female-led shooting plots have been thwarted via tips and successful threat assessment.

When Law Enforcement Takes Action

Elizabeth Lecron made a pilgrimage to Columbine High School, exchanged communication with Charleston shooter Dylann Roof, and planned a mass killing at an upscale bar in my hometown of Toledo, Ohio. Thankfully, her plot was successfully thwarted when local law enforcement and the FBI gave credence to a tip they received from a friend of a male who reported that he was getting seemingly more violent and "changing" under Lecron's influence. A search of Lecron's apartment led to the discovery of instructions and materials to make pipe bombs, several weapons, ammunition, black powder, and dozens of screws, all which would have been used in the initial attack and a second one at a different location.

What's the Motivation?

Just like their male counterparts, female mess shooters seek fame, collect injustices, and wish to seek revenge; many are far too captivated with and knowledgeable of the Columbine attack. They also have high indications of suicidality. They are generally more like their male counterparts than different.

article continues after advertisement

It is important to invest in research toward recognizing at-risk females to help prevent future rampages or targeted shootings. The first step is to understand these shootings and overcome sexism because incidents are growing in number. Regardless of gender, we must be vigilant about warning signs and report concerning behaviors of both males and females at risk of perpetrating devastating acts of violence. We must do all we can to thwart plots, even if that means going against sexist assumptions, media biases, and a lack of information on females' propensity for violence.

item.title: Go Easy With Ambition
item.description:
Motivation

Go Easy With Ambition

Exploring the ancient roots and modern risks of ambition.

Posted October 11, 2026

Key points
  • Ambition's ancient roots link it to seeking honor and power, not just achievement.
  • Excessive ambition may harm trust and collaboration in relationships and teams.
  • True success can be redefined beyond status—toward kindness, impact, and connection.
Source: Miguel Henriques/Unsplash

Ambition sits at the center of how we understand success. As such, we easily ignore its darker elements. A common understanding of ambition includes “drive and determination.” Like any dynamic we revere, it’s easy to conclude that if a little is good, then a lot is wonderful.

Old Understandings

The word ambition's ancient roots may offer meanings that have quietly traveled with it through the ages. One such definition is “going about desiring honor and power.” The phrase “going about” seems to imply a random issuing of overtures hoping to acquire honor and power. As if the identified task at hand is not highly valued, other than its usefulness to promote “power and honor.”

Another old meaning comes from ancient Rome. Ambition described a candidate running for office who sought “favor and goodwill.” The hidden agenda here is likely power, with candidates “going about” seeking their constituency's endorsement.

The Value of Ambition

Being ambitious offers a number of benefits.

  • Energy. Ambition motivates you to start a task or project.
  • Resolve. Ambition can counter lethargy.
  • Enthusiasm. Ambition can encourage others to join a collaborative effort.
  • Planning. Ambition can easily provide the energy needed to create a plan to accomplish a goal.
  • Satisfaction. Ambition can lead to a satisfying achievement, which can easily translate into motivation for future projects. It can also contribute to feelings of self-worth.

Guidelines for Being Ambitious

Whether the “going about desiring honor and power is conscious or unconscious, family members, friends, and colleagues can detect a mission of self-aggrandizement. Consequences may include compromised trust, reduced collaboration, oversight in project management, poor decisions, and unrealistic expectations. Here are some guidelines for being ambitious.

  • Be clear. Be especially clear about how much you’re going about desiring honor and power.
  • Pull your desire off of the task or project. Seek feeling honored and powerful elsewhere.
  • Determination and drive. Focus your determination and drive on the task or project's purpose.
  • Get feedback. Ask for feedback from your life partner, friends, and colleagues regarding their perception of how you’re driving yourself. Being excessively driven can suggest you’re “going about desiring honor and power.”
  • Be gentle. Treat yourself kindly if you notice you’re “going about desiring honor and power.” It’s a natural desire; get the help you need to keep your determination aligned with the project's success.
  • Redefine success. The following is a poem by Ralph Waldo Emerson that does just that, regardless of the intended endeavor.
article continues after advertisement

Success

To laugh often and love much;

To win the respect of intelligent people

and the affection of children;

To earn the approval of honest critics

and endure the betrayal of false friends;

To appreciate beauty;

To find the best in others;

To give of one’s self;

To leave the world a bit better, whether

by a healthy child, a garden patch, or a

redeemed social condition;

To have played and laughed with

enthusiasm and sung with exultation;

To know even one life has breathed

easier because you have lived …

This is to have succeeded.

item.title: Relational Masturbation
item.description:
Masturbation

Relational Masturbation

A third way between intercourse and nothing.

Posted October 11, 2026

Key points
  • Many couples see sexuality as binary: either intercourse or nothing.
  • The truth is that fact that your partner wants sex doesn't mean you need to supply it.
  • Relational masturbation, exploring your own pleasure next to your partner, is a third way to more pleasure.
Source: Hero Images via Canva

Co-authored by Galit Romanelli

Sunday morning. The kids are asleep. Adam and Lily just woke up and are enjoying a lazy morning. Adam wants to have sex. Lily doesn't. She's not in the mood. She's tired. She's preoccupied. Doesn't matter. She loves Adam and truly wants him to be happy, but she just doesn’t want to be sexual now.

Sound familiar?
What would you do?

This is a common situation that we meet every day in the clinic. The situation worsens when the couple's perception of sexuality is binary: either intercourse or nothing.

In our previous post, we described how sensuality is the bridge between the friends and the lovers in intimate relationships. We believe that the wider the sensuality, the richer the sexuality. The same is true in sex: The wider the sexual playground, the more options for mutual pleasure.

Back to Adam and Lily. Here's what we would suggest to Adam:

“How about pleasuring yourself next to her?”

Yes, we're talking about masturbation.

Masturbation Is…

Let's start with a little exercise.
Complete the sentence:


Masturbation is ________.

What's your answer?

I, like many men, grew up with masturbation being something you do alone. Sometimes with a sense of guilt or shame. Oftentimes in the context of porn or other external stimulation. It's not a relational or vulnerable experience.

Women go through a different socialization. As a society, we often frown upon sexual exploration and masturbation for girls and women. We don't talk about it, and that creates a lot of confusion and shame.

In our Honest Intake sessions, we ask every single partner: Do you masturbate? And if so, do you masturbate next to your partner? This is not a science, but roughly 70% of men say that they masturbate, and maybe 10% next to their partner. With women, the percentage is much lower. Around 20% say they masturbate, and about 5% next to their partner. These numbers suggest that many couples are not including masturbation as part of their joint sexual repertoire.

article continues after advertisement

What is masturbation? It’s the process of exploring your own pleasure. It is the sensual experience of one’s joy and gratification.

Between Intercourse and Nothing

We want to invite consensual, respectful relational masturbation as a viable option for couples.

Imagine Adam and Lily expanding their sexual playground with the possibility of relational masturbation: exploring their own pleasure next to their partner. That opens another space to meet as lovers. A third way, somewhere between intercourse and nothing.

Exploring your pleasure next to your partner has several benefits. First, it cuts the emotional umbilical cord, allowing you both to be true to your individual desires without having to be coerced out of them. The fact that your partner wants sex doesn’t necessarily mean that you need to supply it. After all, your partner’s wish is not your command.

Relational masturbation allows your partner to discover a different side of you. They witness another dimension of your pleasure, sensuality, and sexuality. Novelty is sexy. When you bring more dimensions of yourself, your partner will feel free to bring more of themselves too. This effect compounds, creating new, exciting sensual and sexual discoveries.

Finally, it lowers pressure, which is known to be a libido killer. Relational masturbation helps you own your sexuality, and releases your partner from feeling responsible for your pleasure. No one is forced, shamed or pressured into something they don't want. This creates a positive association with sex.

How to do it?

Imagine Adam saying: "Lily, I'm horny and would love to be sexual with you. If I can't be sexual with you, I'd love to be sexual with myself. Is that cool with you?"

Lily has a couple of options.

She can say a positive no, and that’s fine. Adam thanks her for being honest and precise. He can either decide not to, spoon her if she wants, or move away and pleasure himself (which is what most couples do anyway).

She can say fine and go back to sleep. She can say, "I'm happy to watch." She can caress him. She can even give him a hand. So many options.

Imagine the freedom they would gain by having the option of being sexual next to each other. They’ve moved from a binary lose-lose situation to an exciting win-win with many options, just by expanding the sexual playground beyond intercourse.

article continues after advertisement

Where do we start?

Be generous. Make sure your lover feels loved and respected. Invest not just in your sex life, but also as friends and partners.

Talk about it. Galit always says that sex is communicating without clothes. Start the discussion about relational masturbation before the sexual encounter, fully dressed, when the stakes are low. After all, when our clothes are off, our defenses are up. Explore your core beliefs about masturbation and get curious about how you might benefit from expanding the sexual playground.

Know what you like. This is a prerequisite for relational masturbation. You need to own your sexuality and your pleasure. Not sure what you actually like? Never masturbated before? That’s great. Get curious. Become the best lover you've ever had.

Start slowly. After you ask for consent, slowly start exploring your body. It doesn't have to be sexual. It doesn't have to be genital masturbation. Find what feels good next to your partner. Let your partner be privy to seeing you meeting yourself. David Schnarch taught us that intimacy is the process of meeting oneself in the presence of the other. Meeting yourself sensually is a way of revealing more of yourself and deepening your intimacy.

Drop the expectations. Let your partner witness your pleasure without any expectations to engage or reciprocate.

We believe that choice is the new relational hope. By daring to pursue our pleasure within our relationship, we will begin to feel more free together.

Galit Romanelli is a certified relationship coach, Ph.D. candidate in gender studies, and co-creator of The Remarriage Roadmap.

item.title: The Father I Was, the Man I Might Have Been
item.description:
Career

The Father I Was, the Man I Might Have Been

On regretting not only what we denied our children, but what we denied ourselves.

Posted October 11, 2026

Key points
  • Paternal regret can be both interpersonal and self-directed.
  • The ways that fathers unintentionally hurt their children may mirror the ways that they hurt themselves.
  • Fathers who recognize what they have neglected in themselves reclaim crucial aspects of their lost identities.
Source: RuslanSikunov/Pixabay

In my recent posts, we have been focusing on the regret that fathers encounter as their nest begins to empty and they begin to awaken to the difference between the father they were determined to be and the father that their child has been experiencing. We might refer to this as interpersonal regret.

But there is another aspect of regret that is worth considering, as well, one that we might call self-directed regret—the wish that we had chosen to live, relate, and love differently than we have.

All of us will at times encounter regret not only for having failed others, but also for having failed ourselves:

  • I chose my career based on what my parents thought was best, not based on what I thought was best.
  • I stayed in an unhealthy and loveless marriage for far too long because I was too afraid of being on my own.
  • I became overly preoccupied with work because I didn’t want to find out who I was when I wasn’t working.
  • I gave up on being a writer because I never believed I was good enough.
  • My unrelenting anger at my father kept me from spending any time with him and trying to understand him better, and now he’s dead and I no longer have a chance to do so.

There is obviously going to be some overlap between interpersonal regret and self-directed regret when it comes to fatherhood. Feelings of regret might start on an interpersonal dimension—“How did my way of parenting negatively impact my child?”

But these feelings may naturally travel onto a self-directed axis—“How did my way of fathering negatively impact me? What have I lost and what has it cost me to have been the kind of dad I have been?”

So, for example, a father who had workaholic tendencies during his children’s childhood may not only come to regret the fact that he deprived his children of his presence while they were growing up, but also come to regret the fact that he deprived himself by not being present as they grew.

A father who could not tolerate his offspring’s emotional vulnerability may realize that he was simultaneously intolerant of his own emotional vulnerability.

article continues after advertisement

A father who was overly demanding and severe when it came to his expectations of his children may learn that he has been overly demanding and severe when it comes to his expectations of himself.

A father may discover that in becoming estranged from his adult child, he has also become estranged from important parts of himself—qualities that he once hoped would characterize the kind of father he would be.

In other words, many of the fathers who consult with me discover that the very same behavior that may have injured their child also injured them.

From this perspective, we might say that the ache of regret is rooted not just in the kind of parent we have been, but also because we come into contact with the kind of individual whom we have neglected or abandoned but still aspire to be—the father we can still grow toward and ultimately become.

item.title: The Crucial Link Between Anxiety, Anger, and Creativity
item.description:
Anxiety

The Crucial Link Between Anxiety, Anger, and Creativity

What anxiety, anger, and creativity have in common and why it matters.

Posted October 11, 2026

Key points
  • There is a little-understood relationship between anxiety, anger, and creativity.
  • Human beings have a need to create that, when unexpressed, can cause anxiety.
  • Creative self-expression is one of the best ways to productively manage anxiety symptoms.

This is Part 4 of a series on anxiety. See Part 3 here.

Another example of what we as psychotherapists need to convey to our patients seeking relief from their anxiety pertains to the still poorly understood but psychologically crucial connections between anxiety, anger, and creativity.

The Central Role of Psychotherapy in the Treatment of Anxiety

An estimated 470 million people worldwide, according to the World Health Organization, suffer from diagnosed anxiety disorders and many of them receive outpatient treatment such as individual psychotherapy and/or psychopharmacological intervention. Almost 15% of American adults are currently taking some psychiatric medication such as anxiolytics or antidepressants for anxiety (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention). Though antidepressants, unlike benzodiazepines for instance, are not physiologically addictive per se, they can become psychologically addictive—especially when employed as the primary or sole treatment method for anxiety, i.e., instead of psychotherapy.

The purpose of psychotherapy is to educate and help the anxious patient become more aware of the neurobiological, psychological, and existential significance and sources of their anxiety symptoms, and provide tools, techniques, skills, or methods for constructively managing their anxiety. Such tools may include the appropriate use of psychiatric medications to mitigate the severity of their symptoms. But mostly what psychotherapy needs to provide patients are new ways of conceptualizing, coping with, relating to, and managing their anxiety, including methods like meditation, and addressing the connection between anxiety, anger, and creativity. Without such practical assistance, patients come to depend solely upon their psychiatric medications to manage their anxiety symptoms, a treatment approach which, in the long term, typically proves insufficient.

Edvard Munch's "Anxiety."
Source: Edvard Munch/Wikimedia Commons

Anxiety, Anger, and Creativity

What is this nexus between anxiety, anger, and creativity? It is, I submit, what psychologist Rollo May (1969) called the daimonic, which can be briefly defined for our purposes here as the most intense, passionate, and potentially dangerous and destructive emotions that people are capable of feeling and of being temporarily possessed or taken over by at times.

May (1981) writes, "Our culture requires that we repress most of our anger, and, therefore, we are repressing most of our creativity." Much the same may be said of our anxiety. Like anxiety, the passionate emotions of anger, resentment, and rage are pervasive in our culture today. There are myriad reasons for this in our day, but, paradoxically, the primary cause in my view is the chronic repression or denial of the daimonic.

article continues after advertisement

Anger and anxiety are both essential elements of the daimonic. When we chronically deny or suppress daimonic emotions such as anger and anxiety, these feelings intensify, turning pathological, and consequently tend to be experienced and expressed destructively or negatively. In the case of repressed anger, it can fester over time, turning into resentment, embitterment, hostility, hatred, aggression, and violence. (See Diamond, 1996.)

Similarly, chronically suppressed anxiety can intensify and convert into painful and debilitating symptoms such as obsessive-compulsive or panic disorder, phobias, or even the paranoid delusions of psychosis. The chronic repression of anger engenders the experience of anxiety in part because we profoundly fear these "negative" feelings and resist taking personal responsibility for them. Instead, we defensively and unconsciously project or externalize our anger and anxiety outside of ourselves, leading us to feel even more fearful and anxious of others and the world.

The experience of anxiety symptoms can, in our day, frequently be linked to this chronic denial of the daimonic, sometimes signaling the presence of repressed anger roiling just below the surface. In this sense, anxiety, like a fever, can, in general, serve as an indicator of some underlying feeling, emotion, or unconscious inner conflict we need to become more conscious of. Thus, anxiety symptoms can be an indication of repressed anger; and feelings of anger, resentment, or rage can sometimes conceal the presence of underlying anxiety, since, for some, it is easier to accept, feel, and express anger than anxiety, while, for others, the opposite is true.

article continues after advertisement

The Inner Need to be Creative

Creativity is a fundamental, existential, or archetypal human capacity and essential to maintaining mental health. Anxiety, anger, and other daimonic emotions like loneliness, loss, grief, and love are what typically inspire and motivate creativity. Creativity of all kinds can provide comparatively healthy outlets for the constructive expression of both anxiety and anger. Indeed, creativity can be broadly defined as the constructive expression or utilization of the daimonic. (See Diamond, 1996.) For obvious reasons, we tend to fear such powerful, primal passions and, therefore, suppress, deny, and avoid them at all costs whenever possible. This is particularly true of intense affects like anger and anxiety, both of which can, in time, turn into pathological rage or panic attacks and other debilitating and potentially dangerous psychiatric symptoms.

We all—whether artists or not—fundamentally need to creatively express ourselves in the world. Creativity can, and does, occur naturally, universally, perennially, in all people in every walk of life. When such creative self-expression is chronically suppressed, we can become more anxious, irritable, or angry. When a dairy cow is not milked daily, it becomes sick. It is much the same with human beings as regards creativity. We need to create in some way every day. When our creativity is frustrated or blocked, we suffer from symptoms, a condition psychotherapist Otto Rank (1936) referred to as the artiste manque, the artist unable to create.

Chronically unexpressed creativity and the problem of anger, violence, and evil in our culture are closely connected. As Jungian analyst Liliane Frey-Rohn (1967) writes, " ... although creativity is usually evaluated as exclusively positive, the fact is that whenever creative expression becomes an inner necessity, evil is also constellated." If this inner necessity or instinctual drive for creative expression is chronically denied or dismissed, we feel frustrated, angry, anxious, and depressed, and become more susceptible and prone to destructiveness and evil. (See Diamond, 1996, 2026.) This is why creativity—or, at least, constructive activity, self-expression, or productivity—is so essential to ameliorating and managing anxiety rather than merely suppressing it pharmacologically or otherwise. For, in doing so, we are simultaneously suppressing our creative urge. Whether it's cleaning the house, mowing the lawn, cooking a meal, writing a book, painting, journaling, or playing music, channeling or redirecting the instinctual life force of anxiety into constructive activity is crucial.

Conclusion

Confronting rather than suppressing our anxiety opens us up to the deeper channels to creativity. Legendary filmmaker Ingmar Bergman suffered from severe anxiety throughout his life, as have many other great artists such as Herman Melville, Vincent van Gogh, and Jackson Pollock (See Diamond, 1996.) Norwegian artist Edvard Munch expressed his own (and our collective) angst in his controversial paintings. And there are countless other examples of such suffering artists today among the hundreds of millions of ordinary people living with painful anxiety disorders. Creativity, in whatever form, be it artistic or ordinary, is key to coping with and constructively expressing anxiety, anger, and other ubiquitous daimonic emotions in our day and, therefore, must be encouraged in psychotherapy patients whenever possible.

item.title: A Mother With Her Own Needs? Shameful!
item.description:
Career

A Mother With Her Own Needs? Shameful!

Mothers are still harshly judged for caring about themselves.

Posted October 11, 2026

Source: Chat GPT

Not a day goes by when I don’t hear a story like Maggie’s.

Maggie’s 17-year-old daughter was sick; she’d been vomiting for two days and was unable to keep any food down. Having raised a few children and ridden this rodeo many times, her illness presented like a bad stomach virus. (A number of her daughter’s friends were also sick.) On the third evening, her daughter started complaining of bad pain in the center of her belly, at which point Maggie started getting worried, mostly about dehydration. She called the pediatrician.

“This is day three, and you haven’t brought her in yet?” said the female pediatrician. As she put it, “If her daughter could make it through the night, she needed to take her to the office or urgent care first thing in the morning.” The doctor’s tone was disapproving and judgmental.

After hearing the doctor’s comment, Maggie gathered her daughter and headed to urgent care. The doctor there told her that the teen needed to be evaluated for appendicitis—STAT- and so off they went to the emergency room. But after six hours in the hospital, the lab work showed that imaging was not necessary; she should follow up with the pediatrician in the office. That night, she and her daughter returned home at 3 am, which (as an aside) completed a 22-hour day of professional and parenting work for Maggie.

The next day Maggie cancelled her plans and got her daughter to the pediatrician as instructed. The doctor there conducted some tests, but was not alarmed and sent her home with instructions to watch and wait. By now, her daughter was feeling a little better, no longer vomiting, and able to keep a bit of food down. But still, the pain in her belly continued and was not getting better. And so the next day, she took her daughter to the pediatric gynecologist, where the sonogram showed that she had fluid in her abdomen, which was probably what was causing the pain. She told Maggie she needed to be evaluated once again in the ER, for more imaging, since this was serious.

Running on fumes and having missed three days of work, sleep, and food at this point, Maggie asked the female gynecologist if it made sense to call in a prescription for an emergency MRI or CT scan, so they could have it done quickly at the nearby private facility—so they wouldn’t have to spend another day waiting for a scan in the hospital hallways. The gynecologist’s eyes grew large with disbelief; she told Maggie again that her daughter had large amounts of fluid in her belly and needed to be evaluated immediately in a hospital. She also (angrily) added that Maggie would be going directly against medical advice if she pursued any other plan than the one she, as a doctor, was proposing; she would be both doubting her advice and putting her daughter at risk. But then came the real kicker…

For months, Maggie had been working on a critical presentation; if she landed the deal, it would change the trajectory of her entire career and deliver what she’d always wanted. The presentation was scheduled for later that afternoon. Maggie decided to take the risk: She asked, “If we go to the ER you’re suggesting, do you think there’s any chance we’ll be out by 5 pm, or could you speed things along because it’s your hospital?” (It was then 12:30 in the afternoon.) The doctor’s eyes then grew to the size of saucers; if she had been a cartoon character, her eyes would literally have popped out of her animated head. She responded, “You’re asking about your 5 pm meeting?” Dripping with disgust, she went on to inform Maggie that she “had serious concerns” about a parent who rejected medical advice and was asking if she was going to be out of the hospital in time to make her meeting.

article continues after advertisement

And so, Maggie did as she was told, not wanting to be “that” mother about whom the doctor had “serious concerns,” the mother who thought not only of her child, but also about herself, who dared to mention her own needs in the face of her child’s needs. Maggie’s intuition and experience told her to get the scan done outside the ER, though her pediatrician’s office, so she and her daughter wouldn’t have to spend the entire day in the freezing cold hospital. As expected, it took ten hours for an attending radiologist to read the scan, and Maggie and her daughter returned home, antibiotic in hand, at 11 pm. Having “appropriately” missed her meeting, Maggie was now sick with a sore throat, but with the seal of approval that she was a “good mom.” She was also deeply upset, shamed, and angry.

For a woman who loves and is devoted to her child, why is it a crime, a spiritual abomination, for that mother to bring her own needs into the conversation? The harshest judgments (from both women and men) in this society fall on those women who break the silent code of conduct for mothers: the instant a woman becomes a mother, she must disappear, become selfless, admit no needs of her own, and exist solely for the sake of her children. Having needs, her own needs, distinct from her children, is treated as sacrilege, and women are metaphorically burned at the stake for it. That mother is shamed in the public square when she dares to let the genie out of the bottle and admit that she’s still in there, that separate grown-up person who existed before she had children, and who still matters, not only as a mother but as a human being.

It’s 2026, and we’re still horrified and disgusted by a mother who—also—considers her own needs, and who doesn’t solely exist for her children. I wonder, what needs to change to move the dial, so that a mother can admit out loud that she has her own needs, without being dragged through the toxic mud of imposed morality. A good mother and her child can both matter, without it being contradictory or incompatible, and without stripping her of her goodness, compassion, and fierce devotion. It’s not our children—or ourselves—and it’s preposterous and imprisoning that the Kool-Aid we’re drinking hypnotizes us to think it is, and should be.

item.title: Caring and Sharing: A Structured Approach for Couples
item.description:
Relationships

Caring and Sharing: A Structured Approach for Couples

A simple weekly practice that reduces defensiveness and builds intimacy.

Posted October 11, 2026

Key points
  • All couples should schedule a specific hour every week to sit down and talk about what  is and isn't working.
  • Many couples are unable to raise concerns without it quickly descending into a fight.
  • A predictable time to voice concerns precludes frantic urgency to blurt out criticisms the moment they arise.
Source: Mladen Mitrinovic/Shutterstock

I ask nearly every couple I see to do something that sounds difficult in our era of constant multitasking, crazy busyness, and endless crisis management: schedule a specific hour, once a week, to sit down together with telephones off and deliberately talk about what is and isn't working in their relationship.

Most couples resist this at first, since they assume that if they truly loved each other, difficult conversations would simply arise organically whenever something needed to be said. What I've found over 17 years as a therapist is more akin to the opposite: couples who wait for the "right moment" to raise a concern often find the worst moment to vent a grievance or make a suggestion—maybe when their partner is exhausted and already irritated, which all but guarantees defensiveness. A dedicated weekly ritual removes this completely, and it happens to be the exact practice that relationship expert Dr. Warren Farrell spells out in his workshop and book “Role Mate to Soul Mate”. He calls it "caring and sharing.”

Dr. Farrell’s exercise employs a caring and sharing sandwich: two specific appreciations, one clearly stated concern, and two more specific appreciations—always scheduled in advance rather than sprung on a partner in the middle of a hectic week. I love that Dr. Farrell grounds even the scheduling itself in research, citing a Johns Hopkins study in which infants fed on a predictable schedule felt calmer and more secure than infants fed the same amount but at unpredictable times; the children fed willy-nilly ate frantically for fear of not being fed again soon. Similarly with couples, partners who know there’s a predictable time to voice a concern no longer feel the frantic urgency to blurt it out the moment it arises, which is often exactly when it will land worst.

Before either partner shares anything substantive, they remind each other of “The Six Mindsets” that I described previously; the safe space this creates allows the listener to receive criticism without triggering defenses. Dr. Farrell adds that once that non-defensive state is established, there is an equally deliberate structure for the conversation itself and this is the part that works extremely well in session: the sharing partner states their concern specifically, staying focused on feelings that emanate directly from that issue and avoids folding in other grievances. At the same time, the listening partner gives full attention and says “Hold” any time they notice themselves drafting a response instead of simply receiving. When the sharer finishes, the listener reflects back what they heard and asks two questions:

  1. Did I distort anything?
  2. Did I miss anything?

Dr. Farrell emphasizes that the listener continues to refine the reflection until the sharer declares that they feel genuinely understood. Only then does the conversation move to the listener's turn, which requires that the mindsets be refreshed since Dr. Farrell has observed that this altered state of receptivity tends to last only about half an hour.

Many couples come into my office essentially unable to raise concerns without it quickly descending into a fight. I teach them the Caring and Sharing format during our first session and have them commit to a weekly hour. Using the sequence as Dr. Farrell constructed it allows both parties to be vulnerable rather than blamey. They each talk about their emotions rather than focus on their partner’s behavior: this inspires change rather than demanding it, which makes people defensive. Having a weekly safe space to appreciate each other, drop assumptions and authentically work to hear each other’s concerns has improved countless relationships.
